title: The day the wind stopped
hookLine: when baby Hanuman is struck down, his father the wind stops moving and the world can't breathe; sutra 1.34 offers the breath as a door
carry: prana is life; a slow breath out is a door
tomorrow: a man who hated Krishna merges into him. how?

lines: THE SUN LOOKS LIKE A FRUIT.
THE WIND STOPS. NO ONE CAN BREATHE.
cards: As a baby, Hanuman wakes up hungry and sees the rising sun. It looks like a ripe fruit, so he leaps for it.
In the Ramayana's telling, Indra, king of the gods, strikes him with the thunderbolt, and the child falls, his jaw broken; hanu means jaw. His father is Vayu, the wind.
Vayu picks up his son, carries him into a cave, and stops moving. And everywhere, every creature finds it can't breathe.

teach.b: The gods rush to Brahma. Brahma goes to the cave and revives the child, the wind moves again, and the gods heap Hanuman with blessings. That's why he's called Pavanputra, son of the wind.
The story says what Hindu tradition says everywhere: breath is prana, life itself; when it stops, everything stops.

The Chandogya calls breath the eldest and best of the powers, and pranayama, working with the breath, is part of the daily sandhya prayers many Hindus say. Patanjali makes the breath a door for the mind.
Sutra 1.34, in paraphrase: or, by breathing out and holding the breath out.
Prachchhardana, breathing out; vidharana, keeping it out a while. Notice the va again: or. Not a rule for everyone, one more door in the list that began with the four attitudes.
Vyasa reads it as a deliberate breath out through the nostrils and a pause, and calls that holding pranayama, which chapter two takes further.
This lesson keeps it gentle: a long breath out, a small pause, nothing strained.
Now the week, from the top. Bhagiratha: faith and intensity, not talent. Gajendra: a road met from the other side.
Nachiketa's word: say the name, and mean it. Vishvamitra: nine obstacles, all part of the path. The arrow-maker: one thing.
And today, the wind: the door you always carry.

how: Many Hindus begin daily prayer, such as the sandhya, with pranayama, and yoga teachers often introduce sutra 1.34 as a gentle lengthened exhale with a short pause, well before the fuller practices of the second chapter, cautioning students never to strain the breath.

o: a word marking the one required method
a word that offers another way in, not a rule
a word that closes a list of warnings

games.q: the wind, the breath and sutra 1.34.

s: sutra 1.34 says everyone must practice breath control
it begins with va, or: one door among several, not a requirement.
in the Ramayana, when Vayu stopped moving, the world's creatures couldn't breathe
the gods went to Brahma, who revived Hanuman, and the wind moved again.
Vyasa calls the holding in 1.34 pranayama
he reads it as breathing out through the nostrils, then keeping the breath out, and names that holding pranayama.

games.q: your mind is racing and none of the earlier doors is working today. what does sutra 1.34 offer?
o: breathe out slowly and rest in the pause.
hold your breath as long as you can.
games.why: or, by breathing out and holding: Vyasa reads it as a deliberate breath out and a pause with the breath kept out; this lesson keeps it gentle.

practice: If you pray, begin as many Hindus do before puja, with a quiet name of God.

Let the breath be natural for a few rounds, then let each out-breath grow a little longer than the in-breath, slow and easy through the nose, with a moment's rest at the bottom before the next breath comes on its own.
No forcing, no gasping; if you feel any strain, go back to normal breathing.

wordCard.voice: Or. In sutra 1.34, one more door to a clear mind: breathing out, and resting in the pause. Prana, the breath Vayu held back, is the door.

carryVoice: Your line: prana is life; a slow breath out is a door. Hanuman's father taught the whole world that. That's day four hundred forty-one, and a full week.
